The Detroit Pistons face the Giannis-led Miami Heat for the second time this season, but this is not the same Heat team Detroit beat 128-111 in the second game of the season. The Heat can get above .500 with a win after winning six of its past eight games, including the previous three in a row. The Heat are starting to understand how best to play around Giannis Antetokounmpo, especially Bam Adebayo. In the team’s most recent win, Bam and Giannis scored 37 points, and Davion Mitchell was able to support the big two with a 22-point, 17-assist effort.

The Pistons also had Jalen Duren the last time the two teams faced each other, and the big man is still out, and Detroit’s big man is still out recovering from a hamstring injury. Detroit’s big men have been an issue since Duren went down, and that could be an issue when going against both Bam and Giannis. Of course, the Pistons do have Cade Cunningham, and he has vaulted himself into a top-10 player in the NBA. Cunningham is coming off a career-high 52 points and an NBA-first 50-point, 10-assist, zero-turnover game. I’m not sure what he’ll be able to do for an encore, but if the Pistons don’t get decent efforts out of John Collins and Paul Reed, it might not matter.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Wizards final score: Cade makes history in double OT win
pistons.body:
WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 12: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons celebrates against the Washington Wizards during the first overtime at Capital One Arena on November 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Cade Cunningham scored a career-high 52 points, and the Detroit Pistons needed every single one of them in a 144-140 victory in double overtime against the Washington Wizards. It was not just a career-best night for Cunningham, not just one of the top-5 scoring performances in Pistons history, it was the first game in NBA history that saw a player score 50 points, dish 11 assists, and commit zero turnovers.

Cunningham simply did it all. He scored 30 points in the fourth quarter and overtime. That includes a critical 3-pointer after the Wizards had crawled their way back into the lead in the first overtime on an Anthony Davis alley-oop dunk.

The Pistons trailed 130-127 and each team had traded misses. Cunningham calmly took the ball up the left side of the floor, took a pass from Ausar Thompson, and walked into a movement 3-pointer that hit nothing but net to tie the game. On the next possession, Cade swung the ball to Duncan Robinson for what felt like a game-sealing 3 with 9 seconds left, but a video review determined Duncan had approximately 1 milimeter of his foot on the line and changed it to a two.

The scoring barrage also included critical stretch in the fourth quarter where he scored eight points and assisted another to account for 11 of Detroit’s final 12 points of the fourth quarter. Cunningham also locked up Trae Young on defense with Detroit up 119-118 in the final 30 seconds of the fourth. He forced Young into the sideline, cut off any passing lane, deflected the ball, and forced shot clock violation.

Sadly, after Cade hit two free throws to make it a 3-point game, Young redeemed himself by hitting an off-balance three from 29 feet away to give us our two overtimes of fun.

Cunningham’s performance slightly overshadowed another notable feat — Ausar Thompson tallied his first career triple-double. He was aggressive on offense driving to the rim, and delivered crisp passes in narrow lanes to keep Detroit’s offense moving.

On a night where Cade scores 52 and Ausar gets a triple-double, how the heck was it so close to begin with? How does a game like that feature 20 lead changes and 13 ties? It was a weird game.

Alex Sarr was 12-of-14 from the floor and hit his first four threes of the night. He scored 30 points and was one of three Wizards to hit the 30-point threshold. Young scored a team-high 37 points, including a perfect 17-of-17 from the line. Anthony Davis scored 30 points and added 15 rebounds.

Honestly, Detroit’s biggest issue was the same issue they’ve had all season. Their bigs were dominated and DEtroit really misses Jalen Duren. Washington outscored Detroit in the paint and were outrebounded. The biggest issue was John Collins yet again. He was a minus-18 on the night and it felt like it was even worse.

Collins started the overtime period at center in place of Paul Reed, who was a plus-25, and promptly was the primary factor in Detroit giving up a 7-0 run to the Wizards right out of the gate. It was ugly. Come back soon, Jalen Duren.

Yeah, the Pistons might be missing Duren something fierce, but they have Cade Cunningham. And that’s enough.

Rarely have I been so interested in an immediate rematch as I am in tonight’s game, which sees the Detroit Pistons taking on the Washington Wizards for the second consecutive contest. The Pistons prevailed in Monday’s game 122-111. The game was also just dang weird. Anthony Davis played out of his mind, scoring 44 points in just 34 minutes. Rookie AJ Dybantsa also enjoyed the best game of his young pro career, scoring 21 and securing eight rebounds. Everyone else on the Wizards was pretty stinky.

Conversely, Cade Cunningham had one of the worst games of the season, and Detroit was really propelled by some excellent play from John Collins and Daniss Jenkins in a new-look starting lineup. Gone are the mismatched pair of Paul Reed and Collins sharing the floor. In is Collins as a center with room to operate and Jenkins as a secondary ball handler. It’ll be interesting to see if they build off that success or if it was temporary. If Detroit can get both Collins and Jenkins playing at a high level and a locked-in Cade, it could be a blowout. If instead the Wizards bounce back, it could get messy.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Wizards preview:  Round two against the Wizards
pistons.body:
The Pistons and Wizards play each other again, but it is after 3 days of rest for the Pistons and the day after a game for the Wizards because the NBA used Chat GPT to generate the schedule this year or something.  This will only be the Pistons 3rd game in the last 8 days and their 2nd game against the Wizards.

The Pistons were able to control Monday’s game from start-to-finish, but the game was a little closer than it should have been because they had no answer for Anthony Davis.  Davis finished the game with 44 points and only missed 5 shots total.

The Pistons will still be without Jalen Duren, so they once again may struggle to guard Anthony Davis.  But, as Monday proved, even if they can’t stop Davis, they can still win if they stop the rest of the team.

Game Vitals

Where:  Capital One Arena in Washington DC
When:  Thursday, November 12 at 7 pm EST
Watch:  Scripps Sports Network
Odds:  Pistons (-10.5)

Analysis

There isn’t a ton more to say about this matchup that wasn’t very evident in Monday’s game.  With Jalen Duren out, the Pistons have no solution to opposing big men with any kind of offensive skill that are over 6’10”.  It seems hyperbolic, but it really has been the case.  Paul Reed is undersized and John Collins is not a natural center.  Tolu Smith has the size to possibly keep up, but he has proven to be out of his element pretty much any time he has gotten playing time so far.

The Pistons did opt to start John Collins at center against the Wizards on Monday and it did work out offensively, as he had a season-high 24 points.  But, the aforementioned Anthony Davis was able to cruise to 44 points without much resistance.  Anthony Davis always seems to have his best games against the Pistons and I wouldn’t expect him to hit a couple threes every single night, but a lot of the offense he was able to generate was off of offensive rebound putbacks or shots over the undersized players guarding him.

Surprisingly, the Pistons were only outrebounded 46-45, but they were outrebounded 14-11 on the offensive glass.  If you watched the game, you could see the Pistons lack of size rear it’s head countless times.  It is just the current state of things and something the Pistons will have to manage as best as they can for the next two weeks while Jalen Duren is still out with his hamstring injury.

The Pistons benefitted heavily from poor games out of Alex Sarr and Kyshawn George, which George in particular has been arguably the Wizards 2nd best player this season.  Trae Young also had a poor night from beyond the arc where he shot 3-of-10.  Some of that is because of how good the Pistons perimeter defense is and if the Pistons can replicate that tonight, it doesn’t really matter if they have nobody to slow down Anthony Davis.

AJ Dybantsa was able to get going a bit on Monday as he scored 21 points on 8-of-17 shooting.  There were times where he looked overwhelmed, as he had 5 turnovers, but he showed why he was the number 1 pick and a building block for the Wizards.  The Pistons have perimeter players to slow him down, but the refs were very whistle-happy on Monday which helped Dybantsa get momentum on his drives to the basket since the Pistons were not able to be as physical.

One small point of concern has been the play of Cade Cunningham over the last few games.  He had arguably his best game of the season a little over a week ago against the Charlotte Hornets and since then has really struggled, especially from beyond the arc.  He is 1 for his last 19 from beyond the arc after being close to 40% through the first seven games of the season.

He is playing more off-ball and getting clean looks, they just aren’t falling right now.  Teams are obviously focusing their defense more on Cade, but a lot of the current issues are just due to not being able to hit his outside shots.  Hopefully that changes tonight.

Luckily, Daniss Jenkins has been able to step up the last couple nights as he had a career-high, 31 points against the Lakers on Sunday and then 22 points, 6 rebounds, and 8 assists on Monday while starting.  Given the success the Pistons had starting him along with John Collins at center, I would suspect that they roll out that starting lineup again.

There were some issues defensively, which I already touched on, but the offense was much better with Collins starting and more-importantly, it finally got John Collins going after his early-season struggles.

If the Pistons are able to replicate the game they played on Monday, they shouldn’t have a difficult time defeating the Wizards, but if they let one of the other players besides Anthony Davis get hot, the Wizards have a shot at the upset.

Lineups

Detroit Pistons (7-3):  Cade Cunningham, Daniss Jenkins, Duncan Robinson, Ausar Thompson, John Collins

Washington Wizards (4-8):  Trae Young, Kyshawn George, AJ Dybantsa, Anthony Davis, Alex Sarr

Question of the Day

Do you think there is a solution to the Pistons big-man struggles or do they just need to ride it out until Jalen Duren returns?

DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 9: John Collins #20 of the Detroit Pistons dunks the ball in the game against the Washington Wizards on November 9, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Chris Schwegler/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

For those of you DBB sickos who care, I’m officially a married man! We had a spooky wedding on Halloween night and spent the past week in Cabo San Lucas for our honeymoon. We had a great time celebrating over the past week and a half!

Now we’re back to Pistons hoops.

JB Bickerstaff decided to mix up the starting lineup by starting John Collins at center. Paul Reed moved to the bench, and Daniss Jenkins was inserted into the starting lineup. Detroit started small with Duncan Robinson at the 3 and Ausar Thompson at the 4.

It proved to be the right idea early, as Collins was the leading scorer for Detroit after the first quarter with nine points. The Wizards took a 32-31 lead heading into the second, behind 12 points from Trae Young and 11 from Anthony Davis.

Detroit struggled to have an answer defensively for AD, and this was another game where Detroit missed Jalen Duren’s physicality and inside presence. Davis had 30 points and eight rebounds at the halfway point while only missing one of his 11 attempts. The Pistons put up 37 points in the quarter with five different players scoring more than seven points. Collins led the way with 15, Duncan had 14, and Cade had 11 as Detroit held a 68-58 lead.

The third quarter was all about Daniss Jenkins. Cade picked up his fifth foul halfway through the third, and DJ took the reins. He made Trae Young look like a traffic cone on defense as Jenkins went on to score 13 in the quarter. He consistently attacked Young, and Young never stood a chance. Detroit continued to extend their lead as they were up 103-87 heading into the fourth.

The fourth quarter was highlighted by two beautiful plays by Ebuka Okorie and Ausar Thompson.

First, watch Ausar find Okorie in transition as Okorie does his best Kyrie Irving impression:

AUSAR TO EBUKA WE ARE IN HEAVEN pic.twitter.com/jggv5WFEeC
— Rip Haminkton (@RedAlternates) November 10, 2026

Second, the Human Swiss Army knife blocks the 7-footer Alex Sarr on one end, then follows that up by directing traffic and finding an open DJ with a great bounce pass for a wide-open dunk:

Just let Ausar do everything pic.twitter.com/3nlVa0IHKi
— Rip Haminkton (@RedAlternates) November 10, 2026

The Pistons will continue to hope for a speedy recovery for Jalen Duren as they needed his inside physicality against Anthony Davis, who finished with 44 points and 13 rebounds while shooting 16-for-21 from the field. Detroit still managed to pull away with a 122-111 win behind three different players who scored 20+ points, despite none of them being Cade Cunningham.

John Collins, in his starting small-ball five role, led the way with 24 points and 10 rebounds, shooting 9-for-13 from the field. Both Daniss Jenkins and Duncan Robinson added 22 points each, and Jenkins led Detroit with eight assists. Your fun fact of the night: Robinson led the Pistons with seven free throw attempts. There has been a clear difference in his game this year as he looks to get to the line more often. Cunningham added 17 points and seven assists.

The Pistons improve to 7-3 on the season. Detroit’s home-and-home matchup with the Wizards continues as the Pistons will travel to Washington for Round 2 on Thursday night.

Go Stones.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Lakers: Austin Reaves pulls a Doncic to beat Detroit
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 8: Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers drives to the basket during the game against the Detroit Pistons on November 8, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Sevald/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Who needs Luka Doncic when you have the US equivalent from Newark, Arkansas, Austin Reaves? The Los Angeles Lakers guard scored a game-high 43 as his MVP-level teammate rested with a back injury, propelling LA past the Detroit Pistons 121-116.

Honestly, the game had no reason to be as close as it was in the end. The Lakers led 40-14 one basket into the second quarter courtesy of insane shotmaking (hitting 72% from the floor) and an insane amount of Pistons miscues, including having more turnovers (eight) than made baskets (six).

But the Pistons, being the Pistons, weren’t about to give up. While Detroit pulled within one point early in the fourth quarter, the Lakers led wire to wire. So while it was only marginally competitive from Detroit’s point of view, it was certainly an instructive game. Here are some of the things I learned:

1. Kevin Huerter

Kevin Huerter is going to be a critical component of the Pistons’ rotation this season. In a game where Detroit’s entire backcourt didn’t really show up to play (both Cade Cunningham and Duncan Robinson were largely no-shows until some fourth-quarter scoring), Huerter was by far the biggest bright spot for the Pistons.

It also happened to be his best game in a Detroit uniform. Huerter hit four three-pointers, scored 24 points overall, and added five rebounds, five assists, five blocks(?!) and two steals. Ever since the Pistons traded for him at the deadline last season, it was clear Huerter makes winning plays, and you were hoping he’d be able to combine that with rediscovering his 3-point shooting stroke from earlier in his career. The early returns indicate the shot might be back, as well as everything that goes with it. After tonight, he’s hitting 40% from deep this season.

2. John Collins and Paul Reed

Detroit’s starting front court simply does not work, and it will never work. For as long as Jalen Duren remains sidelined or off the floor this season, this is going to be a significant issue for the Pistons. Duren is ramping back up from a hamstring injury and will be out two more weeks. Detroit has been, and will continue to be able to weather that storm. But it ain’t pretty, and any additional time off from Duren will have me significantly worried.

Most will want to pin the blame on the newcomer John Collins, and he has certainly played worse than Reed, but I think it’s the combination that brings out the worst in both players. Each is the kind of big man that relies on the gravity from teammates that allows them to use their athleticism to create the chaos that makes them effective. With both of them on the floor, it’s two bouncy balls pinging around the floor with no semblance of a plan on how to actually get the ball to the rim. The defense is also bad, and the rebounding is even worse. It’s an ugly situation, and it was exacerbated tonight by both men getting out-physicaled by the behemoth seven-footer Walker Kessler. Kessler, the Lakers’ big offseason addition, had 12 points and 16 rebounds, including seven on the offensive end. The Lakers also dominated the Pistons in the paint, 58-46.

Again, the lion’s share of the blame goes to Collins. He’s been quite bad all season, and it’s getting less clear by the day how he’s going to turn it around and be a positive force for the Pistons. I don’t think he’s ever met a 50-50 ball he couldn’t surrender to the opposition. But the pathway to him playing well lies with sharing the floor with Duren. Get well soon, JD.

3. Austin Reaves

The Pistons were correct in trying to give Austin Reaves the bag this offseason. Detroit reportedly was ready to give the wing a max contract this offseason as the second scorer and potential missing piece in a Detroit Pistons title run. Once the Lakers believed the pending RFA had a max offer on the table, they quickly moved to get an agreement to sign him on the eve of free agency so he’d never hit the market.

Reaves was insane tonight. The degree of difficulty on his shots begged belief. He was able to create space, get balanced, and score at all three levels. It was a sight to behold, and he was by far the best player on the floor for either team tonight.

4. Daniss Jenkins

Daniss has that dog in him, especially under two scenarios: 1. There is an impending buzzer. 2. He feels like his team is getting punked. Jenkins was truly the other hero of the game behind Huerter. He hit yet another buzzer-beater tonight, and he scored a career-high 31 points. When the Pistons were down huge, Jenkins got that look in his eye, as if to say, “This is not going to happen.”

From there, Jenkins started firing away from deep, and he was hitting. In the end, he canned eight three-pointers. He was also the ONLY Pistons player to go to the free-throw line more than once in the game. Really, Jenkins is like a better version of Marcus Sasser. He’s got scoring in his blood, and he’s more of an off-guard than a point guard, despite being stuck in a point guard’s body. He’s got three inches on Sasser and better floor vision, so he’s better overall and can cosplay as a point guard better than Sass, but Jenkins works best in this Pistons lineup when he’s not running the offense.

4. The refs.

The referees love the Lakers. Nothing else needs to be said.

lions.headline: Lions vs. Patriots 5 Qs preview: Can Drake Maye clean up turnovers against Detroit in Germany?
lions.body:
Nov 13, 2026; Munich, Germany; An advertisement for the 2026 NFL Munich Game with images of New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez (0) and Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14) at the Zaitoon Market. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

For their first game in 11 days, the Detroit Lions take their show on the road across the Atlantic for an international Week 10 showdown in Munich, Germany, facing off against the defending AFC Champion New England Patriots.

We had the pleasure of connecting with Taylor Kyles, a staff writer for Pats Pulpit, to give us some insight into this New England squad ahead of Sunday morning’s tilt. We learned about the growing concern surrounding Drake Maye’s turnover regression, how injuries have decimated New England’s offensive line, and the coverage busts plaguing an otherwise physical defense—plus how Detroit’s offensive weapons could exploit the Patriots’ secondary in Munich:

1. The Patriots have had a bit of a Jekyll and Hyde season through nine games. It looked like they were hitting their stride after beating the Bills, Raiders, and Jets, but since then, they’ve dropped two of their last three games.

As the defending AFC Champions, what’s most concerning about this uneven start to 2026? What’s there to be encouraged by in their first half of 2026?

The most discouraging thing has been their inconsistency against upper-echelon teams outside of their division. The defense looks great against mid-tier passing attacks, but some of their schematic quirks (not using as much press and man as expected for their personnel, heavy use of disguises, spinning the dial with coverages) have been exposed against the league’s best passers. Drake Maye also regressed to his turnover-prone ways last week after over a month of clean football and MVP-caliber play.

On a positive note, Maye looked good outside of his interceptions last week while fighting for his life against the Packers’ pressure packages, so cutting back on poor decisions and throws should allow him to return to his more recent form. Defensively, they have the players to perform better than what we’ve seen, but I think the coaching staff needs to do a better job putting players in better positions to succeed and potentially simplifying things so players can do what they do best.

2. Drake Maye was six voting points away from being the league’s MVP a season ago, throwing 31 touchdowns to just 8 interceptions. 2026 has seen some pretty volatile play from Maye on a week-to-week basis, leading to him already surpassing his turnover total from a year ago through nine games.

Do you see Maye regressing from a decision-making standpoint, or is his 2026 season a victim of circumstances beyond his control?

A relatively lackluster supporting cast and a banged-up offensive line have made life difficult for Maye. A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs haven’t lived up to expectations when on the field, and blockers Mike Onwenu, Alijah Vera-Tucker, and Reggie Gilliam are all currently on injured reserve. That said, most of Maye’s turnovers resulted from avoidable mistakes, such as forced attempts and throwing the wrong kind of pass for the situation. Maye winning Offensive Player of the Month in October showed he can rise above these issues, but we have yet to see him do it for a truly extended stretch.

3. Injuries have plagued the Patriots all season long. Where do you feel the effects of injuries are hurting this team the most? Who are some players that have made the most out of their newfound opportunities?

Injuries have most profoundly impacted the offensive line. The ground game has been limited due to the loss of both starting guards, forcing the Patriots into being a fairly straightforward downhill rushing attack. Josh McDaniel has tried incorporating different looks and wrinkles, but outside zone hasn’t really been an option with so little chemistry up front. Pass protection held up surprisingly well for a bit, but schemed pressures like blitzes and stunts have become increasingly problematic over the past three weeks, resulting in far too many unblocked pressures. There is hope things will settle down if veteran Greg Van Roten returns from IR, but he’s missed significant time and is one of the oldest players on the team, so how he performs down the stretch is anyone’s guess. Matt Pryor has emerged as a relative bright spot beside Morgan Moses, who’s been dealing with a foot injury for weeks, but the big-bodied guard can be exposed if forced to quickly redirect.

4. New England’s defense is a super interesting read from a statistical perspective. They have one of the most effective pass rushes in the NFL, and their run defense is a top-10 unit at minimum, yet they’re average as a whole unit by DVOA (15th) and below average in EPA/play (23rd).

When the Patriots defense is at its best, what are they doing successfully? Where are New England’s weaknesses on this side of the ball? Are there certain positional matchups, or player archetypes they struggle in defending?

Physicality and discipline stand out most when the Patriots are playing at their best. It’s a veteran group that plays with a lot of pride and attitude, and that translates into players swarming to the football and laying the wood when given the opportunity. Unfortunately, communication lapses and issues against tempo have led to coverage busts and big plays for opposing offenses. The defense has also struggled to take the ball away this season, which has made life tougher for both sides of the ball. This week, I’m worried about their ability to defend Jahmyr Gibbs out of the backfield. New England has yet to face an opponent that truly fed a talented receiving back through the air, but I’m not sure the defense has the linebacker or safety depth to keep Gibbs quiet if Detroit presses the issue. Jameson Williams could also have himself a day if the secondary doesn’t actively disrupt his releases and route stems.

5. The Patriots opened as 2.5-point home underdogs at FanDuel Sportsbook heading into this international matchup against the Lions. What’s one thing you want to see, what’s one thing you need to see, and one thing you’re sure you’ll see happen in this matchup between the Lions and Patriots on Sunday morning our time?

I’d like to see Drake Maye play a clean game and go toe-to-toe with Jared Goff. He had the talent to do so and elevate his supporting cast, but it will ultimately come down to picking his spots and avoiding bad decisions. I need to see a more competitive effort from the defense, particularly in the red area. This feels like a bend-but-don’t-break kind of game, so holding the Lions to field goals will be crucial. Finally, I’m sure I’ll see the Lions move the ball effectively. There are simply too many weapons for the Patriots to defend consistently, particularly without Carlton Davis. Goff will take what the defense gives him and hit a handful of shots, but again, the Patriots must be competitive once the Lions reach the red area.

lions.headline: New England Patriots vs. Detroit Lions preview: 6 key stats
lions.body:
FOXBOROUGH, MA - OCTOBER 09: Detroit Lions running back Jamaal Williams (30) blocks New England Patriots safety Adrian Phillips (21) as Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) prepares to throw a pass during a NFL game between Detroit Lions and New England Patriots on October 9, 2022, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, MA. (Photo by M. Anthony Nesmith/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Holy scheiße! The Detroit Lions’ first overseas game in over a decade, dating back to the early Jim Caldwell era, is finally here, and the Motor City militia is ready to make some noise in Munich, Germany.

While it’s still one of the more compelling European games this season, the buildup is different than expected. The Lions are coming off an emotional week that ended in a low-scoring affair in Miami, while the Patriots were bombarded by Green Bay at home. New England’s season has had its ups and downs, highlighted by a road win in Buffalo, but the team hasn’t found its mojo since the Super Bowl, aside from its head coach this offseason.

Interestingly, the game pits two tough-minded, former-player, CEO-type head coaches against each other. The Lions are looking to extend their four-game winning streak, thanks in large part to their defensive improvements, with their sights set on containing reigning MVP runner-up Drake Maye. They’ll also hope for a much better offensive performance than last time they faced the Patriots, when Bailey Zappe was the quarterback on the other side of the ball, and they got skunked.

So tap the keg and crack a few eggs, as this week’s preview will examine six key stats and matchups Detroit needs to handle to keep the winning streak train on the tracks and let you enjoy your Sunday morning kickoff.

Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus.

Pop Goes The Weasel

The Patriots’ offense heads to Germany with a bit of a MASH unit, as they’ll be down to backup offensive guards Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor. Sending my best regards to those two as they face Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams. They’ll also be without skill-position players Romeo Doubs and TreVeyon Henderson, while A.J. Brown and Rhamondre Stevenson (161 rushing yards vs. the Lions in 2021) are questionable.

Lions fans know not to take a team lightly, even one ravaged by injuries; they only need to look back at Carolina scoring 32 points against them while missing numerous key offensive pieces. Detroit’s defense will still need to shut down the areas opposing offenses plan to attack.

Following Maye’s early-season struggles, which included a 58.6 passer rating, six interceptions, and nine sacks in the first three weeks, he has leaned into fourth-year slot receiver DeMario “Pop” Douglas, despite injuries to Brown and Doubs. Since Week 5, Douglas has recorded 22 receptions for 352 receiving yards and four receiving touchdowns. His receiving yards rank 11th among all players, just two yards fewer than Amon-Ra St. Brown in that span, while his four touchdowns are tied for third. Douglas is a career 11-yards-per-reception player, but he’s averaging 16 yards per reception over that stretch. Douglas has spent a league-leading 81.3% of his snaps in the slot during that span, with the next-closest player at just 72.5%. His 11 receiving first downs from the slot also lead the league over that stretch.

Stopping Douglas will be no easy task for the Lions’ improving defense, as Detroit allows a league-worst +0.59 EPA/pass on targets to the slot. The Lions have faced 101 slot targets (2nd), allowing 8.7 yards/pass (24th), a 10.7-yard average depth of target (30th), seven passing touchdowns (t-28th), and a 60.2% passing success rate on throws to the slot. They’ve also allowed the second-fastest average time to throw on those passes at just 2.45 seconds, nullifying much of the disruption that Aidan Hutchinson, McNeill, and any blitzes can generate.

Stopping Pop Douglas will require a dedicated effort in Kelvin Sheppard’s game plan, with Roger McCreary likely seeing plenty of time trying to burst his bubble, along with help from the linebackers and safeties. Perhaps Brian Branch will see some dedicated time against the small, shifty, but explosive Douglas. If the Lions can keep Pop bottled up in Munich, they’ll go a long way toward cutting off the Patriots’ offensive tap.

The Munich Meat Grinder

The last time the Patriots and Lions faced off, early in Dan Campbell’s second season and potentially a low point of his coaching tenure in Detroit before the team grabbed the rope and started climbing, Rhamondre Stevenson was a problem, particularly running up the middle. He recorded 11 carries for 86 rushing yards (7.8 yards per carry), including a startling 7.8 yards before contact per carry. However, things might be a little different this time around. Whether it’s Stevenson or the more diminutive Corey Kiner attempting to run up the middle against the Lions’ defense, with the aforementioned McNeill and Williams, especially without beefy guards Mike Onwenu and Alijah Vera-Tucker, they might get pounded into schnitzel.

Since Week 5, the Detroit Lions’ defense has allowed a league-best 23.3% rushing success rate on runs up the middle. That also includes just three first downs and zero rushing touchdowns allowed on 30 rushing attempts up the middle. Much like airplanes in America, they’re grounding rushing attacks up the middle.

The Patriots’ offense prefers to run up the gut, with the third-most such carries (96) this season. However, they rank outside the top 10 in yards per rushing attempt (4.1) and just 19th in both EPA/rush (-0.093) and rushing success rate (39.6%). While they rely heavily on running between the tackles, they haven’t been overly successful.

If the Lions can close down the Autobahn up the middle, they’ll force Maye to take the scenic route on third down, where Detroit’s pass rush will be waiting.

The Bavarian Bootleg

Often, when the Patriots run up the middle, they operate from under center, and their 41.5% under-center rate ranks 12th in the league. However, they struggle when Maye is crouched behind second-year pivot Jared Wilson, ranking 27th in the NFL with -0.173 EPA/play from under center. It doesn’t get much better when they use play-action from under center, either.

This season, the Patriots’ under-center play-action passing metrics have been a little startling, as they’re averaging -0.359 EPA/dropback (30th), a 12.7% turnover rate (32nd), a 61.2% completion percentage (22nd), and a 43.6% pressure rate (20th) — despite allowing only one sack.

Longtime offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels hasn’t been able to help unlock Drake Maye and the under-center play-action passing attack, and that’s music to Lions fans’ ears as Detroit continues to adjust to a linebacker corps of Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez (possibly getting more Mike linebacker reps), and Trevor Nowaske, while also acclimating Brian Branch and newly acquired Andre Cisco into the equation. One of those Lions defenders coming up with a turnover, given that Maye has been handing out footballs like beer steins at Oktoberfest with seven turnovers on just 55 under-center play-action dropbacks, would be a welcome gift for Detroit’s overseas success.

Maye-day Parade

Where the Patriots’ offense has been buttering its bread, err, putting the bratwurst in its bun, has been from shotgun, particularly with 11-personnel.

Whether it’s operating from the ‘gun and airing it out to the likes of DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism II, Mack Hollins, and Hunter Henry, or Eli Raridon, Maye has been in an aggressive zone.

From shotgun in 11-personnel, the Patriots’ passing offense has averaged +0.176 EPA/dropback (4th), a 46.7% passing success rate (8th), 8.81 yards per attempt (2nd), an 11.66-yard average depth of target (1st), and a 12.5% explosive pass rate (4th). They’ve also managed to manufacture plenty of time to throw, averaging 3.07 seconds (1st), despite Maye still facing a 49.2% pressure rate (30th) in these situations, similar to Jordan Love at times.

While the Lions’ pass defense has struggled overall against shotgun 11-personnel, allowing +0.084 EPA/dropback (25th) and an 11.6% explosive pass rate (32nd), some metrics have been surprisingly positive. As the defense continues to improve and find itself, Detroit can take confidence in having held opposing offenses to a 42.0% passing success rate (14th), while generating a 45.4% pressure rate (3rd), a 9.0% sack rate (6th), and a 2.2% interception rate (13th) against shotgun 11-personnel passing attacks.

The game could be a lot closer than the Lions would like if Maye gets comfortable spreading the ball around from shotgun with three wide receivers in the formation. But if Detroit can limit the explosive passes and force some negative plays, it might not take 99 red balloons to send the Patriots’ offense into a panic in Munich.

Deutschland’s Favorite Sun (God)

It’s pretty surreal to see Amon-Ra St. Brown in the much-deserved spotlight this week, essentially serving as the Lions’ ambassador to Germany given his heritage. While he’s been disparagingly called a “slot merchant” by lesser talking heads in the past, St. Brown is seeing a career-low slot snap rate of 45.8% this season but has still been feasting when given opportunities from the slot.

On 73 targets to the slot this season, the Patriots have allowed 55 receptions for 690 receiving yards and five touchdowns. They’ve allowed a 75.3% catch rate (30th), 9.45 yards per target (27th), +0.455 EPA/target (27th), a 57.5% passing success rate, and a 16.4% explosive pass rate (29th).

St. Brown is due for a trip to the end zone, having gone five straight games without a touchdown (the referees robbed him of one against the Vikings), and he’ll have an opportunity to shine from the slot against a Patriots defense that has had few answers for opposing slot receivers. With Marcus Jones manning the nickel spot for New England, St. Brown could carve him up in coverage like a finely crafted German wooden nutcracker. Luckily, St. Brown mentioned on Friday that he still has two days to come up with his touchdown celebration.

Achtung! It’s a Pass!

Everyone who’s made it to this portion of the article knows that Jared Goff and the Lions’ offense rip play-action passes like the best of them. And I hate to be the bearer of bad news for the Patriots, but they haven’t been able to stop early-down play-action all season. It’s also a perfect opportunity for Goff to exorcise some lingering Super Bowl demons and exact a little revenge.

The Patriots’ defense has faced 7.9 early-down play-action passes per game, the fifth-most in the league, as opposing offenses have recognized their weakness and are attacking it. On 79 early-down play-action dropbacks, the Patriots’ defense, which will be without Carlton Davis III and features a post-injury-slumping Christian Gonzalez at cornerback, has allowed 51 completions on 71 attempts (71.8% completion percentage, 28th), 10.1 yards per attempt (30th), four passing touchdowns (29th), a league-worst +0.408 EPA/dropback, a 54.9% success rate (25th), and a 16.9% explosive pass rate (29th). Any way you slice it, the Patriots’ defense has been getting diced up on play-action passes.

You can fully expect Drew Petzing to lean into early-down play-action, putting linebackers Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss, along with strong safety Craig Woodson, in a bind while helping mitigate New England’s pass rush. That should create layups for Goff over the middle to his playmakers and potentially loosen up the running lanes for Jahmyr Gibbs, keeping defenders on their heels and in a tizzy early.

lions.headline: Dan Campbell confident Lions’ Germany travel plans will have them ready vs. Patriots
lions.body:
The New England Patriots arrived in Munich, Germany on Thursday morning. The Detroit Lions arrived on Friday morning.

Travel plans for the NFL’s ever-growing international slate have been one of the more hotly debated topics, recently ignited by the Los Angeles Rams’ expedited trip to Australia earlier in the season. They arrived the day before the game and left as soon as it ended. Their opponents, the 49ers, spent an entire week in Australia before the season opener. The Rams got wiped by the 49ers, 27-7, leading many to believe travel plans were at fault for Los Angeles’ lackluster performance.

The difference between the Lions’ and Patriots’ approach to travel is obviously not as drastic. Twenty-four hours may not make that much of a difference, but there are bound to be some who believe the Lions didn’t take enough time to adjust. Lions coach Dan Campbell tried to assure media members in attendance in Munich that they will be more than ready for Sunday’s game.

“Very confident. Very confident. I know today will be the hardest day,” Campbell said.

The last 24 hours have undoubtedly been a grueling schedule for the players. Thursday in Detroit, they had a normal day of meetings, practice, and media availability. Hours later, they were on a flight to Munich, arriving around 8:30 a.m. local time (2:30 a.m. Detroit time). Using whatever energy they recaptured from sleeping on the plane, they went right into team meetings and a walkthrough practice.

“We went from the plane; we have got settled in. About an hour later we have got into meetings, and you’re doing a little bit of the head bob,” Campbell admitted.

Still, with over 48 hours to acclimate before kickoff, Campbell is certain the team will be more than ready for Sunday’s matchup with the Patriots.

“We have got up and moved around, and I know that every eight hours here, we’re going to begin to acclimate,” Campbell said. “I know by the time we hit Sunday morning into that Sunday afternoon game, we’re going to be ready to go. So, we will be primed and ready, and I feel very good about our plan.”

The State Of Our Open Threads - After Oregon

I watched yesterday's game in a resigned silence - I did not expect that we would be Oregon, although for a brief moment, a very brief one, we appeared as though we could maybe at least hang with them for a little while. In the end, 31-7 seemed about right though.
As for the open thread, I think it became obvious, as I was looking at the data last night, that the Michigan State game probably will be the point at which we expended much of our growing frustration, and that the rest of the season will involve many of us feeling as I did yesterday.
In fact, at 2,289 posts, yesterday's thread is the second smallest one so far this season, and for a curbstomping, there was not a lot of profanity relative to times where this has happened in the past. There were only 1,013 instances of tracked words, which in this case would translate to an overall efficiency of 2.26, down significantly from last week's 1.79.

Indeed, if we look at "fuck intensity", which the number of fucks given over the total number of tracked instances, we can see that our classic marker has been on a generally downward trend since Iowa and indeed hit its lowest point this season yesterday. Keep in mind that "fuck" is one of a dozen things that gets tracked, so the space is filled with other terms, but we are definitely giving fewer and fewer fucks as a function of other concerns.

As for fucks specifically, we only gave 156 of them yesterday, down sharply, as you'll note, from the 398 given during the Michigan State game. Shits fell sharply too, from 162 to 69, so it is the same story with those - we gave far fewer. I expect this trend might continue into next week too. We always seem to give a significant amount of both of these for Ohio State though.

It's a similar story here - this part of the fanbase made its feeling known during the MSU game and you can see that "fire" fell from 291 to 133 and that "suck", well, is at 37, so really, if it goes much lower, that is what I call "suck zero", the point at which we objectively inarguably would suck.

We will turn to some of the usual suspects. Again, the mild correlation between "suck" and "offense" continues. It is difficult to show a strong correlation in a season with twelve data points, but, well, sometimes it is rather apparent that, oh, the offense sucks by and large.

Here again, everyone made their feelings known the week before, and when Whittingham was seen miles away from the huddle at one point yesterday, he did his best to confirm those feelings. I want him gone too.

So, yeah, this is kind of what apathy looks like - it happened at the end of 2014 too, after the Minnesota game. "Fire" was still above the mean, but only slightly.

michigan.headline: Position grades from Michigan’s  31-7 loss to Oregon
michigan.body:
EUGENE, OR - NOVEMBER 14: Michigan Wolverines quarterback Bryce Underwood (19) throw the ball during a college football game between the Oregon Ducks and Michigan Wolverines on November 14, 2026 at Autzen Stadium in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Brian Murphy/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

It’s mid-November, and Michigan is officially a .500 football team, dropping to 5-5 on Saturday afternoon to Oregon. It once again wasn’t a pretty performance for the Wolverines. Here’s a look at how each position group graded out.

Quarterback – D

Coming into the game, we knew that Michigan was going to play both quarterbacks. Tommy Carr got the start and played the first two series of the game before Bryce Underwood took over for the rest of the first half, before giving way back to Carr for much of the second half. It didn’t matter. Neither one played well.

Michigan’s quarterbacks combined to complete just 6-of-20 passes for a total of 71 yards. Carr also had nine carries for 43 yards and fumbled once, while Underwood ran for three yards. Even with a new offensive coordinator in charge, Michigan’s passing game made no progress, and it’s proving to be a wasted season for both quarterbacks who have been sorely let down by the offensive staff.

Running Back – B-

For much of the day Michigan seemed to put more of an emphasis on the run game with all three of Michigan’s running backs getting a good amount of work. None of them really emerged to take over the game, but Savion Hiter provided the biggest highlight of the day and arguably the offensive highlight of the year for Michigan with a 70-yard touchdown run in the second quarter.

HITER HOUSES IT 💥

Savion Hiter takes it 70 yards for the @UMichFootball TD.

Watch on FOX pic.twitter.com/np90VIK9xj
— Big Ten Network (@BigTenNetwork) November 14, 2026

Hiter would finish the game with 107 total yards on 13 carries while Bryson Kuzdzal had nine carries for 46 yards and a fumble. Jordan Marshall added five carries for 23 yards. Of note, Marshall has had just 12 carries across the last three games, and it appears that the captain is slowly losing favor in the offense.

Wide Receiver – D+

Michigan’s passing attack did next to nothing in this game, which is to be expected with the quarterbacks being rotated like they were. It also didn’t help that JJ Buchanan left the game with an injury in the first quarter.

Andrew Marsh was the team’s leading receiver on Saturday, hauling in four receptions for 46 yards. He had a chance for a touchdown on a deep ball from Tommy Carr, but was held after beating the defensive back and only benefited from the penalty. No other wide receivers for Michigan recorded a reception on Saturday.

Tight End – C-

It was a very quiet day for the tight end room, as Jalen Hoffman was the lone tight end with a reception, and it came on a third-and-long to pick up the first down with an 18-yard gain. Not much changed with their usage despite Jason Beck no longer calling the offense, so I wouldn’t expect too much from this group going forward with just two games to go

Offensive Line – D+

Michigan’s offensive line didn’t have Blake Frazier once again this week and ended up starting Manuel Beigel at left guard instead of the rhino spot and Marky Walbridge at right tackle. The group also faced the added challenge of having their coach, Jim Harding, serving as the play-caller this week, leaving them with a little less attention on the sideline.

Regardless, it was a bad day at the office for the line as it was unable to protect the quarterbacks and keep Oregon out of the backfield. The Ducks finished the game with three sacks, four tackles for a loss, and five quarterback hurries in what was once again a bummer of a day for a group that hasn’t been able to find its footing all year.

Defensive Line – C+

The defense as a whole had its worst game of the season, and it started up front. Michigan struggled to get any sort of pressure on Oregon quarterback Dylan Raiola, and he was allowed plenty of time in the pocket to improvise and get the ball downfield. Dom Nichols did have a sack, and Jonah Lea’ea did have a tackle for a loss in what was his most productive game of the year.

On the other hand, the defensive line didn’t do a terrible job against the run, allowing 126 yards rushing to the Ducks.

Linebacker – C-

In what was a bad day for the defense, senior Troy Bowles continued his strong play individually, but didn’t get much help from the guys around him in the linebacker room. Bowles left the game with an injury in the first quarter but quickly returned and finished the day with seven tackles. Nathaniel Staehling also added four tackles, while Chase Taylor and Nathaniel Owusu-Boateng had one apiece. Taylor did whiff on an attempt to tackle Oregon running back Dierre Hill’s 49-yard catch-and-run in the fourth quarter.

Defensive Backs – D-

If you want to point the finger at any position group on the defense for Saturday’s loss, it’d be the defensive backs, who really had a hard time with Oregon’s great group of wide receivers. It started on the opening drive when Jyaire Hill was burned on a double move that allowed Jeremiah McClellan to register a 60-yard touchdown. Hill was also beaten by Evan Stewart for a big gain later in the quarter. Additionally, Smith Snowden continued his cold spell by losing Dakorien Moore to get by him for a 59-yard touchdown reception at the end of the first half.

It wasn’t all negatives for the defensive backs as safety Chris Bracy continued his strong play with eight tackles, including one sack.

Special Teams – C+

Michigan’s special teams units didn’t have a spectacular showing either on Saturday. Punter Cam Brown did have an impressive boot to pin down Oregon at the three-yard line in the first quarter, but that’s really where the highlights end. Dierre Hill had a 38-yard kickoff return, while Deakon Tonielli was also flagged for an unnecessary roughness penalty, on which there was perhaps a bit of an acting job on Oregon’s part.

Coaching – F

With the loss, Michigan drops to 5-5, and Saturday’s lifeless loss was yet another poor reflection on head coach Kyle Whittingham. The offensive coordinator change didn’t do anything to spark the offense while the defense had its worst outing of the year, even if Jay Hill’s unit has earned plenty of slack this year. This job continues to look like far too much for Whittingham, who has the Wolverines on the cusp of missing a bowl game for the first time since 2014 (excluding the shortened 2020 season) despite high expectations coming into the year.

Ever since the close loss to Indiana, Michigan has largely been sleepwalking through their last three games, and this season is continuing to spiral into a bad place under Whittingham’s leadership.

Michigan defense getting ready to go out for its second drive pic.twitter.com/DsltDNluGn
— Clayton Sayfie (@CSayf23) November 14, 2026

EUGENE, OR - NOVEMBER 14: Jeremiah McClellan #3 of the Oregon Ducks celebrates a reception during the 1st half of a game between the Michigan Wolverines and Oregon Ducks at Autzen Stadium on November 14, 2026 in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Al Sermeno/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images

The Michigan Wolverines are now 5-5 after losing 31-7 to the Oregon Ducks on Saturday.

Here are key takeaways from Michigan’s loss.

Horrendous passing offense

Why not have a bad passing game with one quarterback when you can have a bad passing game with two quarterbacks? Tommy Carr started the game, but Bryce Underwood relieved him for a bit after two drives and was downright awful. Underwood was 2-of-8 for 26 yards while Carr was 4-of-12 for 45 yards with a lost fumble.

Michigan’s passing offense is anemic, Michigan’s offensive line is horrible in pass protection, and Michigan’s wideouts don’t get open nearly enough. Granted, JJ Buchanan going out early in this one hurt the passing offense, but it’s been one of the worst in the nation even when at full strength.

Worse defensive effort of the season

It was bound to happen — a game where Michigan’s defense had stretches of looking bad. Oregon quarterback Dylan Raiola picked Jyaire Hill and Smith Snowden apart, going 20-of-28 for 341 yards with four touchdowns. Raiola had three long touchdowns — from 60 yards, 59 and 49.

Running back Dierre Hill Jr. also had himself a day, rushing for 98 yards on 21 carries. Michigan’s defense rarely had answers in this one. They’ve kept games close all season long, and this was bound to happen — the bottom finally fell out, and the collective energy/cohesion was not there.

Kyle Whittingham has to be fired soon

A video Clayton Sayfie took from the press box really sums up the coach Kyle Whittingham is — a coach who says he doesn’t like to micromanage. With Michigan’s defense huddled up before its second drive of the game, Whittingham is 30 yards away from the huddle and walking further away from players and coaches.

Michigan defense getting ready to go out for its second drive pic.twitter.com/DsltDNluGn
— Clayton Sayfie (@CSayf23) November 14, 2026

Whittingham is detached from what’s going on. On a play-to-play basis or in the form of a team huddle, he’s not engaged or communicative. Whittingham isn’t a motivator and isn’t really coaching. He’s just… there.

Whittingham has been a good coach in the past, but there’s no reason to believe the version of Whittingham we’re seeing at Michigan is about to do a 180 and turn things around the rest of this season or the next.

The sooner Michigan acknowledges that this hire didn’t work out and it’s not a good fit, the better for both Whittingham and the football program. Whittingham doesn’t have a grasp of Michigan’s traditions, and he doesn’t realize there’s an urgency and hunger to win now, not later.

Whittingham has promised he’s going to figure things out at Michigan, but it’s a hollow promise that’s bound to be one that gets broken. Kyle Whittingham can no longer coach at an adequate level, and to believe that additions to the roster or a better offensive coordinator will greatly change the trajectory of this team feels like a risky exercise. Evidence continues to pile up that Whittingham is a major part of the problem, and if he sticks around in 2027, it’ll only delay the inevitable — his firing.

Michigan is 5-5 and on their way to 5-7 with games left against UCLA and Ohio State. Is it already time to say enough is enough?

Kyle is making sure he get that 25M buyout. Especially after his OC just got 10M to leave.
— Dr. Jalen Anthony Rose (@JalenRose) November 14, 2026

michigan.headline: Michigan Football gets pummeled by Oregon
michigan.body:
EUGENE, OR - NOVEMBER 14: Jeremiah McClellan #3 of the Oregon Ducks runs the ball for a touchdown in the Ducks first possession of a college football game between the Oregon Ducks and the Michigan Wolverines on November 14, 2026, at Autzen Stadium in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Greg Fiore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

The Michigan Wolverines suffered a 31-7 loss at Oregon on Saturday. Michigan’s first year under head coach Kyle Whittingham continues to be a catastrophe, as the Wolverines fall to 5-5 overall and 2-5 in the Big Ten.

Here’s the recap, highlights and stats.

First quarter

It didn’t take very long for Oregon to get on the scoreboard, as quarterback Dylan Raiola connected with wide receiver Jeremiah McClellan for a 60-yard touchdown. The Ducks got out to a 7-0 lead just two minutes into the game.

Dylan Raiola GOES DEEP to Jeremiah McClellan for a 60-yard SCORE!@oregonfootball pic.twitter.com/seTCJNrCQZ
— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) November 14, 2026

Michigan picked up a pair of first downs on its opening drive, but the drive stalled so the Wolverines had to punt.

Oregon continued to pour it on, putting together a 10-play, 64-yard drive to extend the lead to 14-0 in the first quarter. Raiola found running back Da’Juan Riggs for a two-yard touchdown to cap off the drive and completely seize control.

Raiola to Riggs and @oregonfootball tacks on another TD against Michigan pic.twitter.com/ixlm2M5qXL
— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) November 14, 2026

Second quarter

On the first snap of the second quarter, Michigan’s offense finally woke up as running back Savion Hiter sprinted to the house for a season-long 70-yard touchdown run. The Wolverines cut the deficit to 14-7 with 14:49 left in the half.

HITER HOUSES IT 💥

Savion Hiter takes it 70 yards for the @UMichFootball TD.

Watch on FOX pic.twitter.com/np90VIK9xj
— Big Ten Network (@BigTenNetwork) November 14, 2026

It appeared Oregon was going to respond with a score of their own as they quickly marched into the red zone, but Michigan came up with a goal line stand to force a turnover on downs. The Wolverines were in position to trail 14-7 at halftime after showing life in the second quarter, then disaster struck. Michigan allowed Raiola to find wide receiver Dakorien Moore for a 59-yard touchdown with eight seconds left in the half.

Dylan + Dakorien = Ducks TD 🙌

No. 16 @oregonfootball gets a long TD in the final seconds before the half.

Watch on FOX pic.twitter.com/Xn8MNTosEr
— Big Ten Network (@BigTenNetwork) November 14, 2026

HALFTIME: Oregon 21, Michigan 7

Third quarter

On the first drive of the half, Michigan’s offense found a bit of rhythm with Tommy Carr running for 20 yards to move the sticks on third down. However, the Wolverines later went for it on a fourth down and came up empty, turning it over on downs.

Oregon tried to extend the lead, but edge rusher Dom Nichols came up with a big third-down sack to force a field goal attempt. The Ducks missed a 46-yarder, so the lead remained 21-7 midway through the third quarter.

Michigan was hoping to cut the deficit to single digits and get back to within striking distance. The Wolverines finished the quarter with an impressive drive, fueled by running back Bryson Kuzdzal picking up a pair of first downs on the ground.

Fourth quarter

It looked like Michigan was going to get into the end zone, but Carr’s pass to Andrew Marsh on 4th-and-goal went incomplete. Despite going on a 15-play, 69-yard drive that lasted nearly 10 minutes, Michigan somehow had no points to show for it.

The Wolverines needed a touchdown to keep hopes alive on their next possession, but Bryson Kuzdzal lost a fumble for a second straight week to essentially seal the loss. Just for good measure, Carr fumbled it on the following drive.

Oregon added another score, as Raiola threw a screen pass to running back Dierre Hill Jr., who slid through several defenders on his way to a 49-yard touchdown. The Ducks later tacked on a field goal to roll past Michigan.

msu.headline: Cold Weather, Delayed Planes and Another MSU Loss in The Weather Report
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 14: Alessio Milivojevic #11 of the Michigan State Spartans looks to throw the ball during the first half of a college football game against the Washington Huskies at Spartan Stadium on November 14, 2026 in East Lansing, Michigan. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The warm sunny feeling from last week has worn off quickly as MSU returns to the losing column. Frustratingly so, being that they had opportunities, faced a tired and jet lagged Husky squad and very well could have won this game. Even after last week’s victory, MSU fans found it too cold and 10 dollar tickets not enticing enough to show up for a relatively meaningless game. With that said, I better get to the report before fans stop reading.

Sun #1

Suns are always a bit tougher to find in losses. However, my first sun is going to Brandon Tullis. He racked up 21 carries for 84 yards. That is just one less carry than the entire Husky team and four yards shy of doubling their teams total rushing yards. Tullis has been phenomenal the past two weeks getting an opportunity due to injuries. His ability to keep moving forward after contact has been a difference maker in MSU’s ability to slow the game down and with the time of possession battle. Tullis is essentially the third string back and it also makes me wonder about Jace Clarizio. He was highly touted as a big get and the guy can’t seem to get a peek at the field.

Sun #2

My second sun is actually going to the offensive line. They have been the most consistent unit for the Spartans this season. Tullis is getting yards because there are actually holes. A shiftier back may be turning that into more yardage. The line is doing its job though. Giving up one sack and four tackles for losses is such a vast improvement from last year. There’s been four different quarterbacks taking snaps this season, multitudes of running backs and the line just keeps on keeping on. The one unit that had the biggest question marks coming in has shown improvement and consistency. Is it a line that will get MSU places? Not yet, not even close. It is though, trending in the right direction.

Sun #3

My third sun is a bit sad to admit, but for me it rings true. It goes to the ability to stay in games. For the most part this season MSU has managed to remain competitive for more than just a quarter or two. Washington, Northwestern, Illinois are three games that could have gone their way. They gave Notre Dame all they wanted for that game and Notre Dame is a contender for a title this year. This has not been the case in recent years. Granted some of these close losses have been at their own demise and winning those three would make them bowl eligible. If they can manage to stay healthy and pull in some better talent this team will continue to be competitive. The next step of relevance though is winning the close ones and for us as fans in those close ones to not doubt, to feel like the game is in our control. This year it feels like we’re lucky to be hanging but next year, I hope that changes.

Cloud #1

First cloud for me is going to the penalties. The terrible timing of some of these penalties is even more excruciating. The roughing the passer called on a third and forever incomplete pass that allowed Washington to continue their drive and end up going up 14-7 is a prime example. Block in the backs on decent returns, holding on solid first down runs are two others that just killed momentum and were self inflicting ways to guarantee a loss.

Cloud #2

Cloud two is most definitely headed to the turnovers. Both of those turnovers were nails in the coffin. I still have no idea what Fancher was doing on that interception. He’s had enough experience to know sometimes you have to take the sack. Twisting your knee around to throw a Kareem hook-shot into the arms of a Husky defender while you’re driving is not a smart play. Not to mention you almost tear an acl. Gulker’s fumble at the 30 second mark to end the game was almost just as bad. I know the ball was “peanut punched” but you also know that is exactly what every defender is trying to do, especially at that point in the game. I will be honest and admit I did not think they were going to march down the field and tie it up. Fitz may have even tried to go for two. Still, the way the were chipping away down the field started to give some hope until another untimely turnover squelched the game and the season.

Cloud #3

My final cloud goes to the fact that another season is over before Thanksgiving. Too many consecutive seasons without a bowl appearance is unacceptable. Half the country was still wearing masks the last time MSU made a bowl appearance. I have a child that wasn’t even born the last time they went bowling. MSU is better than that. It is a disgrace to be a university of this size and with these resources and have your seasons virtually over by Halloween. I mean, I guess nobody has to worry about freezing their tails off in Spartan Stadium in November but it is also a whole lot more fun to freeze and be relevant. The Oregon game coming up is going to be terrifying. Friday night, prior to Thanksgiving week in front of an empty Stadium on primetime and with the way the Ducks have been airing it out recently, it could be 42-0 at half. MSU needs to figure out how to stay healthy and bring in better athletes.

As always there is plenty more to complain about and perhaps even some extra suns. Maybe our best shot was for planes to have stayed grounded and the game rescheduled to a later date. I enjoy reading your reports in the comments and the discussions that they induce. With our football weather reports ending soon this season, I look forward to your comments on the Washington game. Let’s not kid ourselves though, after victories over weasels and blue devils, we knew we couldn’t keep having nice things, right?

msu.headline: Instant Recap: MSU fails to capitalize, loses to Washington 21-14
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 14: Alessio Milivojevic #11 of the Michigan State Spartans is helped off the field during the first half of a college football game against the Washington Huskies at Spartan Stadium on November 14, 2026 in East Lansing, Michigan. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images

I feel like I need to take a shower after that one. Gross.

The start of the game was fantastic. Two deep throws from Alessio Milivojevic to Bryson Williams and Carson Gulker immediately put Michigan State into Washington territory. After a few direct snaps to Gulker, he punched it in from one yard to put the Spartans up 7-0 early.

The Huskies were able to put together a decent drive to cross midfield, but their 48-yard field goal attempt would miss left to keep MSU up seven. We even got to see Ben Shelton return, though; he seemed to reaggravate his injury and wouldn’t finish the game.

Washington missed on a few deep balls in the first quarter, but Demond Williams Jr. was finally able to connect on one with Chris Lawson for a 58-yard touchdown that would tie the game before the end of the first.

After a few solid throws from Milivojevic, the Spartans were able to get it over midfield, but were forced to punt early in the second. Michigan State’s secondary was struggling as they gave up another touchdown to Lawson, this time for 17 yards to put Washington up 14-7.

MSU saw injuries to Conner Moore and Alessio Milivojevic on back-to-back plays on the next drive. Although Moore would later return in the second half, Milivojevic would not. It was Cam Fancher’s first game back from his injury earlier in the year, and he would play the rest of the game as QB1. Fancher put a nice drive together and found Williams for an incredible catch on fourth down that tied the game at 14 right before halftime.

Both teams’ offenses slowed in the third quarter. Nick Sheridan was putting together a masterclass of a drive near the end of the third, but Fancher made a terrible decision to try throwing the ball away as he was getting sacked, and Washington picked it off in the redzone. This was another game of Michigan State having opportunities to make a play, but always coming up short.

With the game still tied up at 14, the Spartans caught a break after a punt as Washington muffed the catch and MSU recovered in field goal range. However, Liam Boyd missed from 50 yards out, his only attempt of the night.

Washington put a great drive together late in the fourth and scored on a Jayden Limar 1-yard touchdown run with 2:24 left in the game. Fancher did his best to keep the hope alive, including converting two fourth downs, but a pass to Gulker after passing midfield resulted in a catch-and-fumble that ended up in the Huskies’ hands. Washington would hold on to win 21-14.

Something about this game felt icky. The injury bug is still around, the secondary looked terrible in the first half, and it felt like the offense played scared rather than playing to win. Milivojevic threw for 108 yards while Fancher threw for 134. Brandon Tullis handled 21 carries for a solid 82 yards. Both Bryson Williams and Fredrick Moore had four catches for 60+ yards, including a touchdown for Williams. The defense was able to force five sacks, but the explosive Huskies offense was too much in the long run.

Michigan State is now 3-7, and they’ll host the Oregon Ducks on Friday night at Spartan Stadium for an 8PM EST kickoff. After Oregon manhandled the michigan Wolverines 31-7 today, we’ll hope the Spartans can keep it closer than that. The end of the season draws nearer with only two more weeks left for Michigan State.

Go Green!

tigers.headline: Shortstop Angel de los Santos impressed in full season debut
tigers.body:
MIAMI, FL - MARCH 09: A flag bearer presents the flag of the Dominican Republic prior to the 2026 World Baseball Classic Pool D game presented by Capital One between Team Dominican Republic and Team Israel at loanDepot park on Monday, March 9, 2026 in Miami, Florida. (Photo by Kelly Gavin/WBCI/MLB Photos via Getty Images) | MLB Photos via Getty Images

While we wait for more news from the Detroit Tigers this offseason, let’s continue our little series highlighting some of the most interesting breakouts in the farm system this year. We started with first baseman Beau Ankeney. Now let’s take a look at one of the most exciting teenagers in the organization. 18-year-old shortstop Angel de los Santos broke out of the Complex League to make a very impressive debut at the Single-A level.

De los Santos was signed out of the Dominican Republic back in January 2025. He received a solid signing bonus of $387,500 to join the club, and showcased his deep toolkit in a successful campaign in the Dominican Summer League. That got him on the radar last offseason as a name to watch as he arrived stateside. He made good on early reports with an advanced approach, good contact skills, and a nice mix of power, speed, and defensive ability.

De Los Santos didn’t exactly maul Complex League pitching, but in 51 games he hit six homers and struck out just 17.6 percent of the time, slashing .302/.373/.475. Expected to spend the summer in the Complex League, that work, combined with his defensive improvements, convinced the Tigers to push him to A-ball to finish the yeaer. He struck out more after the jump to Single-A Lakeland in late July, but he still hit three homers in 24 games and slashed .234/.314/.362 for the Flying Tigers. All that work got him squarely on the prospect radar, and FanGraphs currently has a 40+ grade on him.

His strikeout rate jumped to 26.7 percent with the Flying Tigers, but he walked 10.5 percent of the time and just didn’t get in enough games to start adapting to a major jump in pitching quality. What I really like is a solid 26.9 percent chase rate, a zone contact rate of 84.2 percent, and a swinging strike rate of 12.9 percent. Those are really good marks for a college hitter debuting, let alone an 18-year-old shortstop.

He did have more trouble with breaking stuff, splitters, and changeups than with fastballs, but that’s par for the course at his age. On the plus side, De Los Santos posted a monstrous .443 wOBA on fastballs over 94 mph. He hits with a pretty level, balanced right-handed swing, utilizing a short kick and he shows the ability to keep the barrel through the zone and can adjust to pitches in flight and still drive the baseball. His recognition against secondary stuff will have to improve, but he shows the raw hitting traits to project that it will.

De Los Santos topped out at 106.7 mph off the bat, so he’s already closing in on average raw power. FanGraphs projects him to eventually reach an above average 55 FV grade in that department. He’s probably added some muscle already to his listed six-foot-one, 161 pound frame, and while he should remain on the slender side and still speedy, there’s plenty of room on his frame to add good muscle in the years ahead.

Between the two levels, De Los Santos stole 30 bases, 10 of them in those 24 Single-A games. He’s not a burner, but he’s quick and gets to above average speed rapidly out of the batters box or on jumps to steal a base.

Defensively, de los Santos has a pretty good glove, quick feet, and an above average throwing arm. His athleticism stands out, and while he makes some mistakes of aggression on balls in play, he’s overall a pretty well rounded shortstop already.

What is harder to convey that the basic details is that de los Santos just feels like a gamer. He’s regularly doing things in all phases of the game to help his team win, and already shows a knack for great at-bats in key situations, catching opponents napping and taking the extra base, and chipping in the occasional run saving web gem. His ceiling is really high. If he had Bryce Rainer’s raw power potential de los Santos would be a top 100 prospect. Even so he looks likely to be a 15-20 homer type of shortstop with an equal number of stolen bases and probably average or a little better defense.

Angel de los Santos is very young, and we’ll need patience, but this is an exciting young talent who will be popping up quite high on Tigers’ prospect lists this year. Cris Rodriguez will continue to draw the most attention among recent Tigers international free agents, but De Los Santos isn’t far behind and has a little stronger floor due to his present contact ability. After so long with no signficant success in the international market for young talent, the Tigers finally seem to be stacking up a lot of interesting talent in A-ball and the rookie ball levels.

Ángel De Los Santos smashes a 3-run homer to left to give Lakeland the lead. It’s his 3rd home run with the Flying Tigers, and his 9th overall this year. pic.twitter.com/2psKDXR4vq
— Tigers ML Report (@tigersMLreport) September 3, 2026
